{{Short description|Category with exactly one morphism between any two objects}}
{{more citations needed|date=February 2024}}
In [[category theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], an '''indiscrete category''' is a [[category (mathematics)|category]] in which there is exactly one [[morphism]] between any two objects.<ref name="auto">{{cite book|last=Crole|first=Roy L.|title=Categories for Types|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mHptq6sqJRIC|page=83|isbn=9780521457019|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|via=Google Books|publication-date=1993|access-date=February 3, 2024}}</ref> Every [[class (set theory)|class]] ''X'' gives rise to an indiscrete category whose objects are the elements of ''X'' such that for any two objects ''A'' and ''B'', there is only one morphism from ''A'' to ''B''. Any two nonempty indiscrete categories are [[equivalence of categories|equivalent]] to each other. The [[functor]] from '''Set''' to '''Cat''' that sends a set to the corresponding indiscrete category is [[adjoint functors|right adjoint]] to the functor that sends a small category to its set of objects.<ref name="auto"/>
